CALM is a secondary protein-input candidate for restaurants with breakfast, bakery, and prepared-food exposure; later layers must separate restaurant demand from egg-price and avian-flu cycles.

CHEF should be tracked as an underfollowed center-of-plate distribution candidate because its filings explicitly mention center-of-the-plate proteins, specialty sourcing, and restaurant customers.

PPC is a cleaner protein-processing candidate than many diversified food companies because it discloses value-added chicken/pork products sold to distributors and foodservice operators, but commodity poultry cycles remain a major confounder.

Need a later pass for private or cooperative restaurant supply-chain entities such as National DCP, OSI Group, Cargill, Koch Foods, Wayne-Sanderson, and other non-public suppliers that may explain hidden dependencies but are not directly investable as US-listed equities.

CHEF is the strongest underfollowed public-market mapping for restaurant center-of-plate protein distribution because it explicitly sells center-of-the-plate proteins to restaurants and culinary customers.

HFFG is a high-relevance but below-threshold speculative exception: niche Asian-restaurant distributor with seafood and meat/poultry exposure, but micro-cap size and control/governance risks require hard verification.

Protein sourcing for restaurants should be split into processor exposure, specialty distributor exposure, and prepared/value-added protein exposure; commodity processors need extra caution because protein cycles can dominate restaurant-demand signals.

CHEF should be retained for Layer 2 as a high-priority underfollowed restaurant supply-chain candidate because it explicitly maps to center-of-the-plate beef, seafood, and poultry distribution rather than only generic foodservice distribution.

HFFG is a speculative shadow candidate below the preferred market-cap threshold; keep only if official filings confirm restaurant customer concentration, meaningful meat/poultry/seafood mix, and acceptable liquidity/governance risk.

The node should include both processors and distributors: custom-cut meat, seafood processing, prepared proteins, and specialty distributor logistics may be closer to restaurant menu execution than commodity packer volume alone.

summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the direct public-company universe for restaurant center-of-plate protein sourcing. The two-lane funnel uses Tyson Foods as the obvious scale reference, then prioritizes less-obvious public exposures in poultry prepared foods, specialty center-of-plate distribution, and egg/protein inputs. Key caveat: many candidates have commodity-cycle exposure, so later layers must separate restaurant-specific value-added demand from generic protein price swings. Expanded the restaurant protein-sourcing node into a focused two-lane public universe. Reference lane anchors include large diversified protein processors, while the underfollowed lane emphasizes companies whose restaurant exposure may be hidden inside foodservice, prepared protein, center-of-plate distribution, or regulated protein-input categories. The best Layer 1B fits are not necessarily pure restaurant stocks; they are processors or distributors whose value-added products, foodservice channels, supply reliability, or protein availability constraints can affect restaurant margins and menu execution. Expanded the node universe toward US-listed protein processors and specialty foodservice distributors with restaurant-facing center-of-plate exposure. The cleanest underfollowed fits are The Chefs' Warehouse for specialty center-of-plate distribution and HF Foods for niche Asian-restaurant seafood/meat distribution, though HF Foods is below the preferred market-cap range and should be treated as a speculative exception.
